newsitem.title: USA: DOLLAR CLOSES LOWER AGAINST MARK IN U.S.
newsitem.headline: DOLLAR CLOSES LOWER AGAINST MARK IN U.S.

text.p: *Dollar holds support at 1.8675 marks, staves off late fund selling in search of stops. Heavy buying of one-week dollar puts at 1.85 also seen. Fresh low set at 1.8660, 1.8650 floor held.
*Stg/mark parks near 2.97 after earlier six-pfennig bloodbath.
*Cable struggles below $1.59 after hitting 1.5780, 10-mo low.
*BoE hikes rates 25 bps but signals near-term tightening over.
The dollar slumped steadily against the mark through U.S. trading but held its ground against the pound and yen after sinking to fresh lows in morning trade.
Sterling tumbled early Thursday after the Bank of England signaled interest rates had risen enough for now, and the dollar fell in sympathy against most leading currencies.
The pound fell to a ten-month low against the dollar and a one-month low against the German mark while the dollar posted its first loss against the mark after surging to a string of eight-year highs.
Dollar/mark struggled to hold 1.87 in afternoon trade as hedge funds tried to muscle the dollar past sell stops toward 1.8650, dealers said.
"We had some large funds trying to bully it around in a summer market," said one New York trader. "There has been some pretty vicious selling today."

The British central bank raised its official interest rate to 7.0 percent from 6.75 percent, its fourth consecutive monthly increase, but released a statement saying it had no immediate plans for future rate rises, triggering heavy selling in sterling, dealers said.

"When they raised interest rates in the morning, they said basically this was the last one and that was the reason sterling went down," said Hans Boman, chief spot currency dealer at Swedbank in New York.

The Bank of England also said the sharp rally in sterling, which had risen 16 percent against the German mark in 1997, was pressuring British businesses by making their goods more expensive in global markets.
Currency dealers said investors had been looking for an opportunity to book profits from the pound's rally and seized on the Bank of England's statement.
"When it comes to sterling, we've all been waiting for this for a long time," said Boman.
The pound touched a low at $1.5780 in morning trade, its weakest since last October, before settling at $1.5870/80, down slightly from the open at $1.5885/95.
The dollar fell to 1.8685/95 marks from 1.8755/60 at the open and edged lower to 118.38/48 yen from 118.39/44 at the open.
Dealers said the pound's decline also gave investors a chance to book profits from the dollar's sharp recent rally.

"We saw sterling lead the way up for the dollar for a long time and now that sterling is coming back down, that undermined the dollar against the mark and yen a bit," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at Bank of Montreal.

Investors also remain watchful for signs of official efforts to stop the dollar's climb, with 1.90 marks and 120 yen considered trigger points for central banks to intervene in the market and sell dollars, dealers said.
Japan has come under heavy pressure for its growing trade surplus with the United States, which is exacerbated by a strong dollar.
German officials worry that a weak mark will lead to domestic inflation and cheapen the value of the single European currency, the euro, slated for launch in 1999.
"The Bundesbank doesn't want the mark to become a worthless currency and it doesn't want the new euro to become a worthless currency," said Johnson.
Yet investors remained eager to buy dollars on any dips, with the healthy U.S. economy drawing heavy capital flows out of Europe and Japan, where economic growth remains feeble.

"A lot of people are happy to see the dollar go down so they can buy it at cheaper levels," said James Powers, vice president for corporate foreign exchange at Westdeutsche Landesbank Girozentrale in New York.
The dollar rose to 1.5300/10 Swiss francs from 1.5275/85 and rose to Canadian $1.3880/85 from C$1.3871/76. The Australian dollar fell to $0.7302/07 from $0.7380/90.
(( --Chris Stetkiewicz, 212-859-1664 ))
